lead: A theodolite measures two angles from one set-up: a horizontal angle between two directions, and a vertical angle above or below the horizontal. It gives true angles only if the lines inside it keep their proper relations. Temporary adjustments make the instrument ready at every station. Permanent adjustments restore those relations when a field test shows one has drifted.
prereq: You need: the level, its bubble and the idea of a line of collimation from the topic on levels and their adjustments in levelling (helpful, not essential).

blocks.text: A transit (vernier) theodolite is built round four lines. The vertical axis is the axis the instrument turns about in azimuth; levelling makes it vertical. The horizontal axis (trunnion axis) is the axis the telescope tilts about. The line of collimation (line of sight) joins the intersection of the cross-hairs to the optical centre of the objective. The axis of the plate level is the tangent to the curve of its vial at the centre of the bubble's run. The axis of the altitude level sets the zero of the vertical circle.

blocks.text: The least count of a vernier is the value of one main-scale division divided by the number of vernier divisions. A circle graduated every 20′ with a 60-division vernier reads to 20′ ÷ 60 = 20″ (a 20″ theodolite). Two verniers 180° apart are read and averaged to remove eccentricity of the circle.

Face left means the vertical circle is on the observer's left when sighting; face right, on the right. Transiting turns the telescope through 180° about the horizontal axis. Swinging turns it about the vertical axis. Changing face is transiting and then swinging through 180° to sight the same point again, so the vertical circle moves to the other side. The mean of a face-left and a face-right observation removes the collimation, trunnion-axis and vertical-index errors.

items: Setting up and centring. Set the tripod over the station, head roughly level, and bring the plumb bob (or optical plummet) over the peg by moving the legs, then the shifting head.

Levelling up. Turn the upper plate until one plate level is parallel to two foot screws. Turn those two screws together, thumbs both moving inward or both outward; the bubble moves the way the left thumb moves. Turn through 90° so the level lies over the third screw and centre the bubble with that screw alone. Repeat until the bubble stays central in every position.
Focusing the eyepiece on the cross-hairs against the sky or a sheet of paper.
Focusing the objective on the target with the focusing screw.
Removing parallax. If the cross-hairs seem to move over the target when the eye moves, the image is not in the plane of the cross-hairs; refocus the objective until it does not.

blocks.text: Centring is checked again after levelling, because levelling moves the head slightly. Modern telescopes focus by moving a lens inside the tube (internal focusing); older ones move the objective on a slide (external focusing).

For a correct theodolite: (1) the plate level axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis; (2) the vertical cross-hair lies in a plane perpendicular to the horizontal axis; (3) the line of collimation is perpendicular to the horizontal axis; (4) the horizontal axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis; (5) the altitude level axis is parallel to the line of collimation, and the vertical circle reads zero when the line of sight is horizontal. The tests are made in that order, because each assumes the earlier relations hold.

items: Plate level test. Level up, then swing the upper plate through 180° about the vertical axis. If the bubble runs n divisions off centre, the error is half of that. Bring the bubble halfway back with the capstan screws at one end of the vial and the other half with the foot screws. Repeat until the bubble stays central in all positions.

Cross-hair ring (vertical hair) test. Sight a well-defined point with one end of the vertical hair and tilt the telescope slowly with the vertical tangent screw. If the point leaves the hair, rotate the diaphragm ring slightly.

Collimation test (horizontal). On level ground set up at O. Face left, sight a point A about 100 m away, transit and mark B about 100 m beyond. Change face, sight A again, transit and mark C beside B. If B and C coincide the line of sight is square to the horizontal axis. If not, BC is four times the error; move the vertical hair with the diaphragm screws until it cuts a point D at one quarter of BC from C.

Spire (horizontal axis) test. Sight a high point such as a spire on face left, depress the telescope and mark a point near the ground; repeat on face right. Two marks mean the horizontal axis is not perpendicular to the vertical axis; one end of it is raised or lowered with the screw in the standard until both faces give one mark.

Vertical circle index and altitude level test. With the altitude bubble centred, the vertical circle should read 0° (or 90° on a zenith circle) when the line of sight is horizontal. Sight a well-defined point on both faces and read the vertical angle. If the two angles differ, keep the hair on the point, set the vernier to the mean angle with the clip (index) screw, and then centre the altitude bubble with its capstan screws.

examples.question: A 20″ transit theodolite is being tested on a level site. (a) After careful levelling the plate bubble runs 4 divisions off centre when the upper plate is swung through 180°. Each division of the vial is 20″. Find the error and state how it is corrected. (b) In the collimation test, with the instrument at O, the marks B and C made 100 m from O on face left and face right are 24 mm apart. Find the collimation error in seconds and say where the vertical hair must be set.
steps: (a) Swinging through 180° reverses the tilted vial about the vertical axis, so the bubble shows twice the error: 4 divisions run means an error of 4 ÷ 2 = 2 divisions.
In angle: 2 × 20″ = 40″ between the plate level axis and the plane perpendicular to the vertical axis.

Correction: bring the bubble back 2 divisions (halfway) with the capstan screws of the plate level, and the remaining 2 divisions with the foot screws. Level again and swing; repeat until the bubble stays central.
(b) Each face throws the line of sight off by 2c after transiting (c on the backsight and c after the transit), and the two faces throw it to opposite sides, so BC = 4c × OB.
Set the vertical hair on D, one quarter of BC from C: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 mm from C towards B. Repeat the test until B and C coincide.
examples.answer: (a) The plate level is out by 2 divisions (40″); correct half with the capstan screws and half with the foot screws. (b) Collimation error about 12″ (0.00006 rad); set the vertical hair 6 mm from C towards B.

traps: Transiting the telescope in the plate level test. The plate bubble is tested by swinging the instrument through 180° about the vertical axis; transiting does not move the plate level.
Correcting the whole bubble run with the capstan screws. Only half the run is the instrument's error; the other half is taken out with the foot screws.
Moving the hair to the midpoint of BC in the collimation test. BC is four times the error, so the hair goes one quarter of BC from C.
Thinking two faces cure everything. The face mean removes collimation, trunnion-axis and index errors, but not a vertical axis that is not vertical; only careful levelling removes that.

quiz.q: Name the fundamental lines of a transit theodolite and the relations they must satisfy.
quiz.a: Vertical axis, horizontal (trunnion) axis, line of collimation, plate level axis and altitude level axis. Plate level axis ⟂ vertical axis; line of collimation ⟂ horizontal axis; horizontal axis ⟂ vertical axis; altitude level axis ∥ line of collimation; vertical hair in a plane ⟂ horizontal axis.

quiz.q: Why must the eyepiece be focused before the objective?
quiz.a: The eyepiece focus puts the cross-hairs where the observer's eye sees them sharply. The objective then brings the target's image into the plane of the cross-hairs. Done the other way, the image and hairs may both look sharp to a strained eye but lie in different planes, leaving parallax.

quiz.q: In a plate level test the bubble runs 3 divisions when the plate is swung through 180°. Each division is 30″. Find the error and the correction.
quiz.a: Error = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 divisions = 45″. Bring the bubble back 1.5 divisions with the capstan screws and 1.5 with the foot screws; repeat.

quiz.q: In the collimation test, marks B and C are 18 mm apart at 90 m. Find the collimation error and the position of D.
A surveyor finds that face-left and face-right horizontal angles differ by 30″ on steep sights but agree on flat ones. Which adjustment is suspect, and why?
quiz.a: The spire test (horizontal axis not perpendicular to the vertical axis). Its effect on a direction grows with tan of the vertical angle, so it is small on flat sights and large on steep ones. A collimation error would grow with sec of the vertical angle and show even on flat sights.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electronic theodolites read encoded glass circles and use a dual-axis compensator that measures the residual tilt of the vertical axis and corrects every reading. Collimation and trunnion-axis errors are measured by a two-face routine and corrected in software; the axes are the same. Search for dual-axis compensator, theodolite collimation calibration and trunnion axis error.

figure.caption: The theodolite seen from the side, with its lines named, and the collimation test of the worked example in plan. The face-left and face-right marks B and C, 100 m from O, are 24 mm apart, so the collimation error is about 12″ and the hair is set 6 mm from C.
